final_recommendation: The room converged on a trilateral package: 70-72-75% RVC phase-in locked permanently, labor-value floor ($14/$15/$16) locked permanently with automatic tariff enforcement, dairy access phased 0.5%-3.25% over five years with the final level renegotiable at year ten, and a year-ten review with year-eleven snapback if talks stall. Canada dropped Chapter 19 in exchange for a trinational enforcement panel with binding remedies and no political override.
minority_objections: Canada initially insisted Chapter 19 was non-negotiable for Parliament
Dairy sector demanded permanent 3.25% access with no year-ten renegotiation
Mexico briefly proposed review-board appeal before tariffs, rejected by Congress
key_conflicts: Chapter 19 dispute settlement: Canada red line vs. U.S. Congress refusal
Dairy permanence: U.S. agriculture demanded locked access vs. Canada needing year-ten flexibility
Labor enforcement mechanism: automatic tariffs vs. review-board appeals
Sunset clause: business uncertainty about year-eleven snapback vs. renegotiation leverage
key_concessions: Canada dropped Chapter 19 demand in exchange for trinational panel with automatic tariff enforcement
U.S. accepted dairy final level renegotiable at year ten (schedule locked)
Mexico accepted automatic tariffs without review-board appeal
All parties accepted 70-72-75% RVC phase-in instead of immediate 75%
Canada accepted labor-value floor locked permanently
red_lines: Canada: Chapter 19 initially, then shifted to binding dispute mechanism with automatic enforcement
U.S. Congress: no Chapter 19, automatic tariff triggers without political override
Dairy sector: 3.25% market access commitment (achieved via locked schedule)
Labor unions: permanent labor-value floor with automatic enforcement
Auto industry: RVC ramp locked permanently with no year-ten walk-back
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Supply-chain compliance costs during three-year RVC phase-in received acknowledgment but minimal mitigation beyond the phase-in itself
Year-eleven snapback risk to capital investment plans was confirmed but not softened (no grace period during stalled talks)
Political feasibility in Parliament of accepting permanent labor floor while keeping dairy negotiable was assumed, not validated
downstream_risk_variables: Parliamentary ratification in Canada with Chapter 19 removed and dairy partially open
Congressional ratification with dairy level renegotiable at year ten
Actual enforcement of labor inspections and automatic tariff triggers in practice
Year-ten renegotiation dynamics with dairy and potentially labor floor back on table
Supply-chain adjustment costs and timeline compression during 70-72-75% transition
uncertainty_notes: The final package leaves unresolved: (1) whether Canada's Parliament will actually ratify without Chapter 19 despite the trinational panel substitute, (2) whether the year-ten renegotiation of dairy final level creates a new crisis or functions smoothly, (3) how automatic tariff enforcement will work operationally when violations are found, and (4) whether the year-eleven snapback creates sufficient investment certainty or freezes capital plans.

marker_evidence.auto_rules_bottleneck: 75% RVC and phase-in structure drove concrete proposals (70-72-75 ramp), concessions (phase-in instead of day-one), and was stated reason for capital commitment decisions by auto industry and supply-chain manufacturers
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_key: Labor enforcement mechanism (automatic tariffs, 60-day trigger, no review board) was the primary stated reason Congress would ratify, drove Mexico's concession to drop review-board appeal, and was locked permanently as condition for trilateral signature
marker_evidence.canada_dairy_final_issue: Dairy was extensively discussed and drove the 0.5%-3.25% phase-in proposal, but it did not block the deal—Canada accepted the locked schedule with year-ten renegotiation of final level, so it was a consideration but not decisive
marker_evidence.dispute_settlement_canada_redline: Chapter 19 was Canada's opening red line ('not signing anything' without it), drove the trinational panel compromise with automatic enforcement, and was the primary stated reason Canada shifted position—materially shaped the outcome
marker_evidence.sunset_to_review_compromise: Year-ten review with year-eleven snapback was the specific compromise that resolved business uncertainty (supply-chain manufacturers stated it enabled capital commitment), and USTR drafted binding text in response to this pressure
marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congressional ratification constraints drove multiple concrete outcomes: rejection of Chapter 19, demand for automatic tariffs, rejection of review-board appeals, and requirement for permanent labor floor—stated repeatedly as reason for U.S. positions
marker_evidence.supply_chain_adjustment: Supply-chain compliance costs and sourcing timelines were raised by auto industry and supply-chain manufacturers as concerns (60-day remediation window, six-month procurement cycles), but the only mitigation was the phase-in itself—acknowledged but did not change the 75% target or enforcement timeline
marker_evidence.us_mexico_first_pressures_canada: The U.S.-Mexico bilateral was mentioned as leverage (USTR: 'we do the bilateral with Mexico and Canada joins later'), but Canada's actual concessions were driven by the trinational panel substitute and dairy compromise, not by bilateral threat alone—raised as background pressure but not the decisive factor
